There is genuine disagreement among experts and research on whether crying at work is unprofessional. On one side, a clinical psychologist and survey data indicate that crying at work is "seen as unprofessional in general," with 32% of workers saying it is never OK, and criers often labeled as weak, unprofessional, or even manipulative [d1]. Research by UC Davis professor Kimberly Elsbach found that crying can damage careers, with tearful people seen as warmer but less competent, and a peer-reviewed study on physicians similarly rated workplace crying as "slightly inappropriate and unprofessional, ineffective for the work process, and weak" [d2][d7]. Business etiquette expert Barbara Pachter also states that "crying is generally not acceptable in the office," except in specific circumstances like receiving difficult news [d8]. On the other side, a 2018 study found that about 74% of CFOs in the United States said crying at work is OK from time to time or has no negative effect on career prospects [d4]. Dr. Catherine McKinley of Tulane University argues that emotions like crying are "understandable and perhaps unavoidable" at work, and experts at humanpsychology.com.au contend that "it should not be viewed as unprofessional to cry at work," noting it is inconsistent that anger and frustration are accepted while crying is excessively punished [d3][d5]. In sum, whether crying at work is considered unprofessional depends heavily on workplace culture, frequency, and context, with credible research and expert opinion falling on both sides of the debate [d1][d4][d7].
